text: Keep an adjective only when it adds a fact the noun does not carry; a precise noun needs no colour around it.
check: Every adjective left in the rewrite carries a fact (a place, a size, a tool, a date); evaluative ones with no fact behind them, such as 'excelente' or 'increíble', are cut.

text: Know what the message has to get before writing its first word; the opening and the close weigh the most.
check: The first sentence states the purpose and the last one asks for or confirms a single next step.

text: Say each thing with the plain words that state it exactly; do not swap them for rarer synonyms or for the sound of the sentence.
check: No word of the original was replaced by a rarer synonym, and a key term keeps the same word each time it appears.

text: Tell only what the reader needs to act on, one fact after another; cut the sentence that repeats or decorates.
check: No fact appears twice, and every sentence that was cut held no fact (facts-preserved).

text: Say the action with its verb, not with an abstract noun and an empty verb: 'migré los mails', not 'realicé la migración de los mails'.
check: slop-lint OFI-01 does not fire where the genre turns it on; no 'realizar la', 'llevar a cabo la' or 'efectuar la' before a noun in -ción or -miento.

text: Alternate short and long sentences; a run of sentences of the same length reads flat.
check: slop-lint EST-11 does not fire on a text of eight or more sentences.

text: Put the request or the news in the first sentence and the context after it.
check: The first sentence names what the writer asks for or reports; no opening about the writer's feelings or the weather.

text: In rioplatense Spanish, keep the treatment the writer used (usted or ustedes stay); when the writer addresses one person informally, use vos and its direct verbs ('podés', 'tenés que'), never tú, as the Argentine state's own site does.
check: The rewrite keeps the treatment of the original (voice-kept); no 'usted' or 'tú' forms appear where the original used vos.

text: Write the way you would tell it to the person in front of you: common words in their natural order, no stock formulas.
check: No stock formula such as 'me pongo en contacto con usted' or 'quedo a su entera disposición'; the judge's same-voice rubric holds.

text: In a casual WhatsApp message, write the way people from Buenos Aires talk: short clauses, vos, everyday words, and none of the formulas of a letter.
check: No letter greeting or closing ('Estimado', 'Saludos cordiales'); voseo kept; no 'che', slang or emoji that the original did not have (voice-kept).

text: Do not imitate the period language of the literary sources: no archaisms and no pronoun fused onto a conjugated verb ('díjole', 'hállase', 'quedose').
check: S6 finds none of the terms; the judge's literary-contamination rubric flags any other archaism.

text: Do not add literary ornament: no stacked adjectives, no metaphors and no lyrical images in a message about work.
check: The judge's literary-contamination rubric finds no ornament the original did not have.

text: Do not chain clauses into a long period; when a sentence carries two ideas, split it.
check: No sentence of the rewrite is longer than the longest sentence of the original; the judge's literary-contamination rubric holds.

text: In an email, a follow-up or a cover letter, no lunfardo and no loose spoken syntax, even in rioplatense Spanish.
check: S6 finds none of the terms; the judge's register-fit rubric holds.

text: Do not take the tone of a story: no fatalism, no drama and no irony at the reader's expense.
check: The judge's literary-contamination and register-fit rubrics find no tragic or sardonic turn the original did not have.

text: Open on the reader, not on yourself: the role, the need or the plan of theirs that made you write ('Te escribo porque vi que la escuela quiere renovar el sitio'), taken from the original or the posting, before any achievement of yours.
check: The first paragraph names the reader's organisation, role, need or the earlier contact, using only what the original or the posting says, and no achievement or metric of the writer appears before it.

text: Say in one plain sentence what you want to bring them or help them with ('me gustaría ayudarlos con eso'), before you give the evidence; it states an intention and adds no fact.
check: Before the first achievement there is one sentence of intention that points at the reader's need; it holds no number, client, tool or result that the original or the CV lacks (facts-preserved).

text: Put each achievement next to the need of theirs it answers, in the same sentence or the one before; an achievement told for its own sake reads like reciting the CV.
check: Every sentence with an achievement or a metric is tied, by a clause or by the sentence before it, to a need, requirement or plan of the reader named in the text; no bare list of achievements without a lead-in.

text: The letter is not the CV in fewer words: it gives what the CV cannot, why you write to them, what you want to do there and how one example relates to their need, and leaves the rest of the history to the CV.
check: Judge question: does the text give the reader something the CV alone does not (the reason for writing, the intention, the link between an example and their need), or is it the CV in fewer words? A rewrite that only lists CV items fails.

text: Lead into your experience with a short bridge that says why you are telling it, and link one paragraph to the next with a word that carries the logic ('por eso', 'además', 'en ese sentido'); a transition that links nothing is filler.
check: A bridge sentence that refers to the reader's need or to the intention comes before the first achievement; each transition names a relation between the parts it joins, and slop-lint reports no stock filler opener such as 'en el dinámico mundo actual'.

text: In a neutral rioplatense email, the bridge can be as plain as 'Te cuento lo que hice últimamente, a ver si te sirve para lo de ustedes': it announces the examples and ties them to the reader in the writer's own voice.
check: When the original uses vos, the bridge before the first achievement uses vos too and names the reader's matter ('lo de ustedes', the project, the role); no 'me permito comentarle' or other stock formula.

text: In a first contact, close with a polite, open offer: you are happy to talk or to send more, when it suits them ('la semana que viene o cuando te quede cómodo'). Do not set the day for them ('¿Lo vemos el viernes?') or announce that you will call.
check: In a first contact the last paragraph names no fixed weekday, date or hour chosen by the writer and no 'te llamo'; it offers availability or more information and thanks the reader. A day the original already agreed with the reader stays.

text: A follow-up first recalls the earlier contact and what it was about ('Te escribo para retomar la charla por el puesto de soporte'), then adds the one thing left to say and asks lightly about the next step or the timeline they gave.
check: The first sentence refers to the previous message or conversation; the close asks about the next step or the timeline without a deadline set by the writer.

text: Be warm and courteous without selling: thank the reader, keep a natural tone without losing formality, and let the facts speak instead of praise of yourself.
check: The text thanks the reader or acknowledges their time once; no self-praise without a fact behind it ('apasionado', 'altamente capacitado', 'llevar al siguiente nivel'); the judge's same-voice rubric holds.

text: A cover letter has room for three to five short paragraphs, about one page; spend it on the why, the intention and the links, not on more CV items, and stop before it is longer than the reader will read.
check: The cover letter stays within one page (about 400 words at most) and the words it gains over the original go to the opening, the intention and the bridges, never to facts the original lacks.
